# colvmn — Full Documentation

Site build: colvmn · 2026-11-13 · 8a3c744

colvmn (pronounced column) is a tiny layout engine for static sites. Pages are described by an _index.md with YAML frontmatter, or an _index.json. The engine renders each page to static HTML at build time and to live DOM in the browser, so content is visible to JavaScript-free crawlers and to readers with JavaScript enabled.

See also: /llms.txt (curated index) and /sitemap.xml.



---

<!-- Page: (root) -->
Source: /

A minimal static-site layout engine.

colvmn (pronounced *column*) is a tiny layout engine for static sites. Pages are described by an `_index.md` with YAML frontmatter, or an `_index.json`. The engine renders each page to static HTML at build time and to live DOM in the browser, so content is visible to JavaScript-free crawlers and to readers with JavaScript enabled.

This page is itself generated by colvmn — the engine is self-hosting, with no recursive submodule.

### Features

- **LLM-friendly** — `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, and `sitemap.xml` are emitted on every build. Pages and folders can be left out of the llms files, and an optional build stamp names the commit they reflect.
- **Scheduled updates** — a folder with an `_update.md` refreshes its own page on a schedule, or when what it watches changes, by running a script or a Claude prompt, and commits the result or opens a pull request.
- **AI reviews** — opt in any page, add an API key or two, and Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok review it and everything below it from its own docs, published unedited and redone when the docs change.
- **Markdown or JSON** — write pages as `_index.md` with YAML frontmatter, or as structured `_index.json`.
- **Pre-rendered HTML** — content is visible to crawlers, AI agents, and JavaScript-disabled clients without waiting for the engine to run.
- **Identical client and build paths** — the same renderer runs in Node and in the browser, so static and live output match.
- **Structured content blocks** — cards, tables, timelines, FAQs, key/value pairs, lists, images, slideshows, collapsed sections, and an auto-generated table of contents.
- **Inherited page metadata** — `topTitle`, parent titles, and back-links are walked up the directory tree automatically.
- **Readable from `file://`** — engine asset URLs are rewritten to page-relative paths so generated pages render locally without a web server. JavaScript-driven features (live re-render, dynamic fetches) require a server, but pre-rendered content, styling, and navigation work directly from disk.

- **Quick Start** — Add colvmn and create your first page.
- **How It Works** — Build- and runtime rendering, and generated outputs.
- **Authoring** — Markdown vs JSON, page metadata, and content blocks.
- **Scheduled Updates** — Pages that refresh themselves: update files, triggers, credentials, publishing.
- **AI Reviews** — AI models review any page and what's below it, from its docs, unedited, kept current.
- [GitHub](https://github.com/stevedekorte/colvmn) — Source code (MIT).


---

<!-- Page: ai-reviews -->
Source: /ai-reviews/

---
title: AI Reviews
subtitle: Any page can have Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok review it and everything below it, from its own docs. One setting on the page and an API key; colvmn does the rest.
---

AI reviews belong to a page. A page that opts in gets reviews of its folder and everything below it: opt in the root page to review the whole site, or a guide, tutorial or reference to review just that. Each model's first answer is published unedited, next to the page, and redone when those docs or the model change. colvmn finds the models, asks them, writes the pages and keeps the history.

## Setting it up

Opt in each page whose folder should be reviewed, in its frontmatter (or `"aiReviews": true` in its `_index.json`):

```markdown
---
aiReviews: true
---
```

And name the reviews folder once, in the site's `colvmn.json`:

```json
"aiReviews": { "folder": "AI Reviews" }
```

The root is a page like any other: opt it in to review the whole site. Opting in isn't inherited, so a page under an opted-in page has reviews of its own only if it opts in too. Reviewing a folder of one short page says little; the root and a few big sections are where reviews are worth having.

Give the runner at least one key, as an environment variable or in `_credentials/NAME.secret.txt` at the site root, and run it on a schedule (see [Scheduled Updates](../scheduled-updates/index.html)). The keys are the providers' standard ones, shared with any other job that uses them:

| Key | Provider |
| --- | --- |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Anthropic |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | OpenAI |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | Google |
| `XAI_API_KEY` | xAI |

To keep the reviews' spending apart, give them keys of their own with `keys`: `"keys": { "Claude": "CLAUDE_REVIEW_KEY" }`. A provider without a key is skipped, and its card says it hasn't been reviewed yet.

Turn on `buildStamp` too: each review then quotes the stamp of the docs it read, which shows which version it reviewed, and whether it read them at all.

## What gets reviewed

A page's reviews cover its folder and everything below it, minus every reviews folder in it:

- **The root** is reviewed from the site's `llms-full.txt`.
- **Any other page** is reviewed from its own `llms-full.txt`, which the build writes next to it with only that folder's pages. With `buildStamp`, it carries its own stamp: the last commit that touched a page in that folder.

A parent's review therefore also covers its opted-in children's content. Each review says which build it read, and each page's reviews sit with that page:

```
docs/Guide/
    _index.md           aiReviews: true
    llms-full.txt       this folder's pages, for its reviews
    AI Reviews/
        _index.md       the reviews page: one card per model
        Claude/         the current review, and archive/
        ChatGPT/
        Gemini/
        Grok/
```

## What happens

The runner adds a job of its own. It runs once a month (set `schedule` to change that), and each run has two steps:

1. **Choose the models.** For each provider with a key, colvmn reads the provider's model list from its API. Claude, with web search, then reads the providers' own announcements and chooses each one's newest, most capable model from that list. Names alone can't tell: they change shape between generations (Gemini 4 is "Argon", "Carbon" and "Hydrogen"). Only an ID from the provider's own list is accepted, and a provider Claude can't choose for is skipped, never guessed. The choice is made once per run and shared by every page; it is recorded, with the page each choice is based on, in `AI Reviews/_models/models.json` at the site root. This needs the Claude key, and costs a few cents.
2. **Review, page by page.** A provider whose current review of a page was made from the same docs, model and prompt is skipped, so editing one guide re-reviews only that guide and the pages above it, and a month with no new docs and no new model costs only the model check. Otherwise its model is sent the prompt with that page's `llms-full.txt` attached, and its answer is published as written: the previous review moves to the archive and the new one is committed.

To check before paying for reviews, run the first step alone, one provider, or one page: `node colvmn/update/ai/reviews.js --models`, `--only Gemini`, or `--scope docs/Guide` (`.` for the root). Each review sends the whole of that page's `llms-full.txt`, so its cost grows with its docs: for about 200,000 tokens, roughly one to three dollars per model.

The first time, each reviews page is written with default text. Edit it as you like.

## The pages

- **The page itself.** A link to its reviews, **AI reviews →**, on the page's footer line, once the first review exists.
- **The reviews page** (`<page>/AI Reviews/`). "AI reviews of this section's content on {date}", where `{date}` becomes the latest review's date. Then one card per model: its full name and its one-sentence verdict.
- **A review page.** The model, date and verdict, the review, then **Details**, closed until clicked: the model ID, the build stamp the model quoted, the exact prompt with a link that opens it in that model's own app, and a line saying it isn't an endorsement by the provider. Then earlier reviews.

Every reviews folder is left out of `llms.txt` and every `llms-full.txt`, so a model reviewing the site never reads earlier reviews.

## The prompt

A page's own `prompt` (in its frontmatter) comes first, then the site's `prompt` in `colvmn.json`, then a default:

- **The root** asks the model to read the site's `llms.txt` and the pages it links, ignore the AI Reviews, and evaluate the site's subject: what it is, its strengths, weaknesses and risks, who should and shouldn't use it, and how it compares to alternatives.
- **Any other page** asks it to read that page's `llms-full.txt` and evaluate that section the same way.

A section often deserves its own question: `prompt: Evaluate this guide: is it accurate, clear and complete, and who is it for?`

colvmn adds two lines asking the answer to begin with the build stamp the model saw and a verdict of at most 20 words. It reads both from the answer: the stamp shows which version of the docs was reviewed (and whether the model read them at all), and the verdict is the model's card text.

## Settings

On a page:

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `aiReviews` | `true` has this page's folder reviewed. Not inherited. |
| `prompt` | This page's review prompt, before the two lines colvmn adds. |

In `colvmn.json`'s `aiReviews`:

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `folder` | The reviews subfolder's name in each opted-in folder. The only one required. |
| `prompt` | The default prompt for every opted-in page. |
| `providers` | Default `["Claude", "ChatGPT", "Gemini", "Grok"]`. `{ "name": "Claude", "model": "<id>" }` pins a model instead of having it chosen. Another provider is `{ "name", "company", "app", "ask" }` (`ask` is a URL with `{prompt}`); it can be shown, not produced. |
| `homeCard` | `true` also adds a card for the root's reviews to the root page's last card grid. |
| `schedule` | How often the job runs: `monthly` by default, or `weekly`, `daily` or a cron string. A run with nothing new costs only the model check. |
| `keys` | A key name per provider, instead of its standard one: `{ "Claude": "CLAUDE_REVIEW_KEY" }`. |

The build warns while `aiReviews` is set but no page opts in.

## From site-wide reviews

Before reviews were per page, a site had one section at `AI Reviews/` in its root. That is where the root's reviews live now, so opting in the root page keeps its reviews, archives and URLs. The old `about` setting and its Review Process page are gone, since each review's Details show its prompt; the build warns while `about` is set.

## Corrections

A review is never edited. To correct a fact, add an `## Author's note` section after it; it stays until that review is replaced. A review page's frontmatter also takes `share`, a link to the same prompt answered in the model's own app, shown as "View the original conversation".


---

<!-- Page: authoring -->
Source: /authoring/

---
title: Authoring
---

Every page is a directory with two files: a thin `index.html` shell and a content file. The content file is either Markdown (`_index.md`) or JSON (`_index.json`) — both compile to the same page model, so the choice is about convenience, not capability.

## Markdown or JSON

Reach for `_index.md` on prose-heavy pages: YAML frontmatter for metadata, then ordinary markdown. The parser turns each `##` section into a `ContentText` block, so a markdown page is really just a convenient way to write a sequence of text blocks.

Reach for `_index.json` when a page needs structure markdown can't express — a card grid, a table, a two-column layout, or a specific mix of blocks. The same blocks are also available from a `content` array in markdown frontmatter, but that array *replaces* the markdown body rather than merging with it, so pick one authoring path per page.

## Page metadata

The same top-level keys work in markdown frontmatter and at the top of `_index.json`:

| Key | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | The page heading. An empty string hides it — useful on the root, where only the brand shows. |
| `topTitle` | The brand shown at the top of every page; inherited down the directory tree when unset. |
| `subtitle` | A tagline rendered just under the header. |
| `content` | An array of content blocks. In JSON this is the body; in markdown frontmatter it replaces the body. |
| `llms` | `false` leaves the page and everything under it out of `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`. It is still generated and in the sitemap. |
| `aiReviews` | `true` has AI models review this page's folder (see [AI Reviews](../ai-reviews/index.html)). `prompt` sets its review prompt. Not inherited. |
| `footerLinks` | `[{ "title": "…", "href": "…" }]`: links on one line at the left of the page footer, separated by middle dots. The AI reviews link joins them. |
| `nextSectionLink` | `true` adds a footer link to the next sibling in the parent's cards, or up to the parent after the last one. |

## Content blocks

A block is an object with a `type` and its own fields. Any block may also carry a `content` array of nested child blocks.

| Block | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ContentText` | Headings, paragraphs, prose sections |
| `ContentCards` | Grid of linked cards |
| `ContentTable` | Tables with headers, rows, and an optional note |
| `ContentImage` | One image |
| `ContentSlideshow` | Images that crossfade in one frame |
| `ContentUnorderedList` | Bulleted lists |
| `ContentOrderedList` | Numbered lists |
| `ContentKeyValue` | Key/value pairs |
| `ContentTimeline` | Dated entries on a horizontal timeline |
| `ContentFAQ` | Question/answer entries |
| `ContentToc` | Table of contents (usually generated automatically) |

Markdown pages produce `ContentText` blocks automatically; the rest are written in JSON or a frontmatter `content` array.

## Images, slideshows and collapsed sections

These need no JSON: markdown marks them with a Pandoc-style `{…}` suffix.

**Zoomable images.** Append `{.colvmn-zoomable-image}` to an image to have a click open it full size:

```markdown
![Architecture](images/arch.svg){.colvmn-zoomable-image}
```

**Slideshows.** Mark consecutive images `{.slideshow}` to show them in one frame that crossfades between them:

```markdown
![Light cycles on the grid](images/cycles.jpg){.slideshow .autoplay}
![The maze from above](images/maze.jpg){.slideshow}
```

With a mouse, arrows fade in at the image's left and right edges; on a touch screen, a tap on either half moves. Arrow keys, swipes and trackpad swipes work too, and a click on the middle enlarges the image. Below it, ‹ 1 / 2 › shows where you are. Two options, as classes on any of its images: `.autoplay` advances by itself every few seconds while it's on screen (pausing while you hover or interact), and `.no-controls` hides the ‹ 1 / 2 › line. Without JavaScript, and in print, the images are stacked.

**Collapsed sections.** Mark a section's heading `{.collapsed}` to have it start closed:

```markdown
## Details {.collapsed}
```

The heading becomes a button with a plus that turns to a minus as the section slides open. A link to the section opens it. Without JavaScript, and in print, it shows open. In JSON, set `"collapsed": true` on a top-level `ContentText` block.

Both markers are left out of `llms-full.txt`.

### ContentText

The default block. `body` is raw HTML; markdown sections compile to exactly this.

```json
{
  "type": "ContentText",
  "title": "Overview",
  "body": "<p>Plain HTML, with <code>inline code</code> and <a href=\"#\">links</a>.</p>"
}
```

Set `"layout": "2 column"` to render the title as a left-hand label beside the body.

### ContentCards

A grid of cards. `columns` is optional (it defaults to the item count, capped at 3). Items come in three forms:

```json
{
  "type": "ContentCards",
  "columns": 2,
  "items": [
    "quick-start",
    { "folder": "how-it-works", "title": "How It Works", "subtitle": "The build and runtime model." },
    { "href": "https://github.com/stevedekorte/colvmn", "title": "GitHub", "subtitle": "Source code.", "arrow": "Visit" }
  ]
}
```

- A bare string is a **folder card**; its title and subtitle are read from that subfolder's own `_index`.
- An object with `folder` is a folder card with an explicit `title` and `subtitle`.
- An object with `href` is a **link card** to any URL; `arrow` sets the call-to-action label (it defaults to "View").

### ContentSlideshow

The JSON form of a slideshow. `autoplay` (default `false`) advances by itself; `"controls": false` hides the ‹ 1 / 2 › line.

```json
{
  "type": "ContentSlideshow",
  "autoplay": true,
  "images": [
    { "src": "images/cycles.jpg", "alt": "Light cycles on the grid" },
    { "src": "images/maze.jpg", "alt": "The maze from above" }
  ]
}
```

### ContentTable

```json
{
  "type": "ContentTable",
  "columns": ["Block", "Purpose"],
  "rows": [
    ["ContentText", "Prose sections"],
    ["ContentCards", "Grid of linked cards"]
  ],
  "note": "An optional italic footnote."
}
```

A cell may itself be an array of strings, which renders as a bulleted list inside the cell.

### Lists, key/value, FAQ, timeline

```json
{ "type": "ContentUnorderedList", "title": "Features", "items": ["First", "Second"] }
```
```json
{ "type": "ContentKeyValue", "items": { "License": "MIT", "Language": "JavaScript" } }
```
```json
{ "type": "ContentFAQ", "items": [ { "q": "Why colvmn?", "a": "Small, pre-rendered, no build framework." } ] }
```
```json
{ "type": "ContentTimeline", "items": [ { "date": "2024-01", "title": "First release", "href": "..." } ] }
```

## Adding a block type

New block types drop in by extending `ContentBase` and registering them in `layout.js` and `static-gen.js`.


---

<!-- Page: how-it-works -->
Source: /how-it-works/

---
title: How It Works
---

Each page is a directory containing two files: a thin `index.html` shell and an `_index.md` or `_index.json` holding the content. Nesting these directories builds the site tree — a `ContentCards` block auto-populates from subfolders, back-links point at the parent page, and `topTitle` is inherited down the tree. (See Authoring for the content formats and block types.)

At build time, `static-gen.js` walks the site tree, finds every directory that has both `index.html` and an `_index.md` (or `_index.json`), runs the layout engine against each one, and writes the rendered HTML back into `index.html`. At runtime, `layout.js` does the same thing in the browser, replacing the pre-rendered content with a freshly rendered copy. The two paths produce identical output.

The generator also writes:

- `sitemap.xml` — every page URL
- `llms.txt` — a curated index for LLM agents
- `llms-full.txt` — the full site content as markdown, one page per section

When the optional `colvmn.json` at the site root sets `siteUrl`, canonical `<link>` tags and absolute sitemap entries are emitted. Its `llmsExclude` list, and a page's `llms: false`, leave pages out of the llms files; `buildStamp: true` adds a line naming the last commit that changed an included page.

A folder with its own `colvmn/static-gen.js` is a **nested site**: a site of its own inside another, such as a project's docs. The enclosing site's build renders it as its own site, with its own `topTitle` and back-links, and keeps its pages out of the enclosing site's llms files and build stamp; they stay in the sitemap. Its colvmn must be the same version as the root's, or the build stops and says so.

## Generating

Regenerate the static HTML, `sitemap.xml`, `llms.txt`, and `llms-full.txt` from the site root:

```
node colvmn/static-gen.js
```

colvmn can also render its own pages without being a submodule of itself, by passing the site root explicitly:

```
node static-gen.js .
```

In that case the root `index.html` references `./style.css` and `./layout/layout.js` directly instead of `/colvmn/...`.


---

<!-- Page: quick-start -->
Source: /quick-start/

---
title: Quick Start
---

Add colvmn to your site as a submodule:

```
git submodule add https://github.com/stevedekorte/colvmn.git colvmn
```

Make each page a directory with two files. `index.html` is a thin shell:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/colvmn/style.css">
<title>My Page</title>
</head>
<body>
<div class="page"></div>
<script src="/colvmn/layout/layout.js" type="module"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

`_index.md` holds the content:

```markdown
---
title: My Page
topTitle: My Site
subtitle: A short tagline for the page.
---


---

<!-- Page: scheduled-updates -->
Source: /scheduled-updates/

---
title: Scheduled Updates
subtitle: Pages that refresh themselves. A folder with an update file runs a script or a prompt on a schedule, or when what it watches changes, and publishes the result.
---

Some pages go stale unless someone remembers to update them: reports, figures, generated reference pages. colvmn's update runner keeps them current. Put an `_update.md` in a page's folder; the runner decides when it is due, runs it, checks what it changed, rebuilds the pages and commits the result, or opens a pull request for review.

## The update file

Its frontmatter says when the job runs and what it may change. Its body is the prompt for a prompt job, or a note for a script job.

```markdown
---
schedule: weekly            # daily, weekly, monthly, or a cron string (UTC)
writes: ["Competition/**"]  # what the run may change; default: the job's folder
publish: pr                 # pr (review first) or direct
model: claude-sonnet-5-5
budget: 1.00                # dollars per run; a hard stop
---
Research the products listed below. Update each one's card:
pricing, recent launches, notable reviews. Cite sources.
```

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schedule` | `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, or a five-field cron string, in UTC. |
| `on` | `push`: run when the site's main branch is pushed, instead of on a schedule. |
| `watch` | Folders or globs, from the site root. The job runs only if one changed since its last run. Works with either trigger. |
| `minInterval` | The least time between runs: `12h`, `30d`, `2w`. |
| `run` | A script to run with Node, from the job's folder. Without it, the job is a prompt job. |
| `writes` | Globs the run may change, from the site root. Anything else fails the run. |
| `publish` | `direct` commits on the current branch; `pr` commits on a branch and opens a pull request. Default `pr`. |
| `secrets` | Credentials a script job is given, by name. Prompt jobs may not have any. |
| `model`, `budget` | For prompt jobs: the Claude model, and the most a run may spend. |
| `notify` | Which results this job emails about: `failure`, `changed`, `nothing` or `all`. Overrides the site's setting. |
| `target` | The page the job refreshes; default the folder's `_index.md`. |

## When a job runs

A job runs when its **trigger** fires (its schedule comes round, or a push), it is past its **minInterval**, and something it **watches** has changed. Any part left out is no condition.

```yaml
on: push
watch: ["source"]        # a folder means everything under it
run: classTree.js
```

A job's own output never counts as a change to what it watches, so a job can't make itself due. Another job's output does count, which is how one job triggers another: a cheap daily job writes `models.json`, and a costlier job that watches it runs only when it changes.

## Script jobs

A script job runs `node <script>` in its folder. It gets a minimal environment: `PATH`, `HOME` and locale, the credentials it lists, and these:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `COLVMN_SITE_ROOT` | The site root. |
| `COLVMN_JOB_FOLDER` | The job's folder, from the site root. |
| `COLVMN_LAST_RUN`, `COLVMN_LAST_COMMIT` | When the job last ran, and the commit it started from. |
| `COLVMN_NOTHING_TO_DO` | The exit status that means "nothing to do" (3). |

Its exit status says what happened: `0`, done; `3`, nothing to do (its changes are discarded and nothing is recorded, so the run leaves no trace); anything else, failed. Numbers belong in scripts: they give the same answer every time and can't make a figure up.

## Prompt jobs

A prompt job runs Claude Code headless in the site root, with the job's prompt. It has no shell. It can read, search the web and fetch pages, and edit only what `writes` allows. Its `budget` is a hard stop, and its cost is recorded and shown in notifications. It uses the runner's own `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, never a job credential, so a web page that tells the model to send a key somewhere has no key to send.

## After a run

1. Every changed file must match `writes`.
2. The site's pages are rebuilt.
3. No changed file may contain a credential value the job was given.
4. The run is recorded in `_update.state.json` beside the update file.
5. The change is published: committed (`direct`), or committed on the branch `colvmn-update/<folder>` and opened as a pull request (`pr`). While that branch exists, the job waits rather than open another.

If any check fails, the run's changes are discarded. The runner only starts from a clean working tree, so discarding restores it exactly.

## Credentials

A credential is described once, by a file named after it, in a `_credentials` folder at the site root or in a folder above the job:

```json
{ "about": "Stripe restricted key, read-only", "pattern": "^rk_" }
```

saved as `_credentials/STRIPE_READ_KEY.json`. The nearest description wins; `{ "blocked": true }` refuses the credential to everything below it. Being described is not being given: a job gets only what it lists in `secrets`.

The value comes from the environment variable of the same name when it is set (for example a GitHub Actions secret), else from `_credentials/STRIPE_READ_KEY.secret.txt` beside the description, which must be ignored by git or encrypted with git-crypt: add `_credentials/*.secret.txt` to the site's `.gitignore`. colvmn won't read a value file git could commit, the build fails while one exists, and the runner never stages or cleans these files. A description can check the value's format with `pattern` (a regular expression) or `"format": "json"`. Problems name the credential, never its value.

colvmn describes the AI providers' standard keys itself: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY` and `XAI_API_KEY`. Any job can list them in `secrets` with no description file; they need only a value. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is also the runner's own key for prompt jobs.

Keep every key read-only and narrowly scoped, so the worst a leak exposes is figures that were headed for the site anyway.

## Running it

```bash
node colvmn/update.js --dry-run              # every job: due or not, and what it would be given
node colvmn/update.js                        # run the scheduled jobs that are due
node colvmn/update.js --on push              # run the push jobs whose watched paths changed
node colvmn/update.js --folder Competition   # run one job now, due or not
node colvmn/update.js --push                 # ... and push the commits and open pull requests
```

To run on a schedule on your own Mac, copy `colvmn/update/launchd-template.plist` to `~/Library/LaunchAgents/`, fill in the site's path and the keys, and load it with `launchctl` (the file says how). Once a day it pulls, runs the due jobs and the push jobs whose watched paths changed, and pushes what they commit. Give it a checkout you don't edit in, since the runner won't start on uncommitted changes. The keys stay in that file, outside the repo.

To run on GitHub Actions instead, copy `colvmn/update/workflow-template.yml` to `.github/workflows/` in the site's repo and add the secrets it names. It runs the due jobs daily and the push jobs on each push. Commits pushed with the workflow's own token don't start new runs, so the runner's commits can't trigger it again.

## Built-in jobs

A site whose `colvmn.json` has `aiReviews` gets a job without writing any update file: it has Claude choose each AI provider's latest top model, then has those models review the pages that opt in. See [AI Reviews](../ai-reviews/index.html).

## Notifications

The runner can email a summary after it runs. Turn it on in the site's `colvmn.json`:

```json
"updates": {
    "notify": { "on": ["failure", "changed"] }
}
```

`on` takes `failure`, `changed`, `nothing` or `all`, and a job can override it with `notify`. One email covers the whole run: each job's result, message, cost, changed files and commit, and a link to the run's log. The addresses and the sending key are credentials, `NOTIFY_EMAIL_TO`, `NOTIFY_EMAIL_FROM` and `RESEND_API_KEY` by default (rename them with `to`, `from` and `key`), so no address is in the repo. Mail is sent through Resend. An email that would contain a credential value is withheld.
